One of my old teammates commented on the story I shared that the Discord bot had been in the works for years.

I told him: you should see it now.

I will get to the parts where it starts looking like a game. There was an ASCII era, a simple voxel era, and then the assets that finally made the invisible work visible.

But if I am going to peel this project back one layer at a time, the first layer is character creation.

Configuration-driven choices are overrated.

I say that as someone who loves configuration.

The character creator started with the open-source D&D project at dnd5eapi.co. The Mastodon adventure bot already used it. Its hosted API had aggressive rate limits, but you could run the project locally. It was good enough for that bot, so it was good enough for mine.

Then I tried to make a Monk.

One tool-proficiency prompt was a choice whose options were themselves choices, each opening another array of options. The data was valid. My generic character creator still had to execute its control flow.

I still do not know whether the model was wrong for what I wanted or whether I fell short of finding the right interpreter. I honestly thought I could conquer it. It got too messy.

The breakthrough was a much less ambitious question:

What if I just coded what a Fighter gets?

The D&D rulebook could state its grants and the decisions it required. Manual options were easier to understand and gave me more freedom than the generic version.

Then ToData changed everything.

Loading a character became: get its data from the repository, call LoadFromData, and now you have a fully functioning character. Saving became: call ToData and send the result back.

A repository stores data. A rulebook restores behavior. The API moves between them.

This is the first architecture field note behind the game:

https://kirkdiggler.github.io/rpg-toolkit/

We had solved how to create and save a Barbarian.

Well, Rage is part of that data, right?

That is where the next field note begins.
